subject: Computer Networking
title: From URL to Rendered Page
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on From URL to Rendered Page.

hook.text: Type a URL, press Enter, and a page appears. Behind that moment are dozens of steps in milliseconds.

buildup.text: The browser resolves DNS, opens a TCP connection, performs a TLS handshake, then sends the HTTP request.

discovery.text: The server responds with HTML. The browser parses it into a DOM tree, then fetches CSS, JS, and images.

twist.text: CSS blocks rendering until it's parsed. JS blocks parsing unless marked async or defer. Order matters hugely.

climax.text: The render tree combines DOM and CSSOM. The browser calculates layout, paints pixels, and composites layers.

punchline.text: URL to pixels in under a second. A symphony of protocols.

quiz.question: What blocks HTML parsing in the browser by default?
options: JavaScript that is not marked async or defer
Image files referenced in the HTML

details.summary: When you enter a URL, the browser resolves DNS, opens a TCP connection, performs a TLS handshake, sends an HTTP request, receives HTML, parses it into a DOM, fetches CSS and JavaScript, computes styles and layout, and paints pixels. This pipeline completes in milliseconds for fast sites.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding the critical rendering path reveals where performance bottlenecks occur. Each step offers optimization opportunities that determine whether a page loads instantly or frustratingly slowly.
takeaways: DNS, TCP, TLS, and HTTP happen before the first byte arrives
HTML parsing, CSS styling, layout, and paint produce visible content
Render-blocking resources delay the first meaningful paint

faq.question: What is the critical rendering path?
faq.answer: The critical rendering path is the sequence of steps a browser takes to convert HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into visible pixels. It includes DOM construction, CSSOM construction, render tree building, layout, and paint.

faq.question: What are render-blocking resources?
faq.answer: CSS files and synchronous JavaScript block rendering because the browser needs them to calculate visual layout. The browser pauses rendering until these resources are downloaded and processed. Deferring non-critical JavaScript, inlining critical CSS, and using async loading minimize render blocking.
